title: Nepal’s climate test: What an earlier adaptation push could have changed - The Business Standard
description: Nepal’s climate test: What an earlier adaptation push could have changed  The Business Standard
publisher.title: The Business Standard
full_article:
Nepal has become a global symbol of climate vulnerability. From devastating floods and landslides in mountain communities to glacial lake outburst risks and increasingly erratic monsoon patterns, the country faces a growing disaster burden. While Nepal has made notable progress in disaster preparedness and climate policy, recent disasters show that adaptation efforts continue to lag behind the scale and speed of climate impacts.

The Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA), established under the Paris Agreement and advanced through the UAE Framework for Global Climate Resilience, was designed to address precisely these gaps. Had robust GGA targets and indicators been agreed, financed and implemented earlier, Nepal could have been better prepared to reduce disaster losses and protect vulnerable communities.

The GGA aims to strengthen adaptive capacity and resilience while reducing vulnerability to climate change. Unlike mitigation, which focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, adaptation seeks to help communities cope with the impacts of a changing climate. For countries such as Nepal, adaptation is not a future necessity but a present development imperative. Stronger adaptation systems can translate directly into lives saved, infrastructure protected and livelihoods preserved.

One of the most significant benefits of an earlier operationalised GGA for Nepal could have been stronger early warning systems. Many floods and landslides have affected remote communities where timely information and evacuation mechanisms remain inadequate. Global adaptation targets focused on universal early warning coverage could have helped mobilise greater investment in weather monitoring stations, community-based alert systems and digital forecasting technologies. Earlier warnings would have given households, schools and local governments more time to act before disasters struck, potentially reducing casualties and economic losses.

A second area is climate-resilient infrastructure planning. Nepal's mountainous terrain makes roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and settlements particularly vulnerable to extreme rainfall and landslides. If GGA targets had encouraged systematic climate-risk screening of public investments, infrastructure projects could have been designed and maintained to withstand increasing climate risks more effectively.

The GGA could also have strengthened local adaptation planning. Nepal has pioneered local adaptation plans of action, yet implementation remains constrained by limited resources and technical capacity. Clear global adaptation benchmarks, backed by predictable financing, could have provided municipalities and provincial authorities with greater support to translate local plans into action.

Another critical area is climate finance. If ambitious GGA indicators had been accompanied by stronger commitments from international partners, Nepal could have had access to larger and more predictable flows of adaptation finance. This would have been particularly important for local governments, which often face the consequences of climate-related disasters while having limited fiscal and technical capacity to prepare for them.

Ecosystems also have an important role to play. Forests, wetlands and watersheds can act as natural buffers against floods, erosion and landslides. Integrating ecosystem-based adaptation into development and land-use planning could therefore help Nepal address disaster risks while protecting natural systems that communities depend on.

The central lesson is that adaptation cannot remain a long-term ambition. Had comprehensive GGA targets, indicators and financing arrangements been operationalised earlier, Nepal could have entered recent disasters with stronger preparedness systems, more resilient infrastructure and better protection for vulnerable communities. The evolving GGA framework now offers an opportunity to turn those lessons into concrete national action.

What Nepal should do now

Nepal should develop national GGA indicators that are closely aligned with measurable disaster-risk reduction outcomes. These indicators should not remain standalone climate targets; they should be integrated into national development planning and linked to clear responsibilities for federal, provincial and local governments.

googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display("dfp-ad-tbs_lb_snd_mobile3"); });

Climate-risk screening should also become a standard requirement for public infrastructure projects. Roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, settlements and other major investments should be assessed against current and projected climate risks before construction and periodically throughout their operational life. This would help ensure that infrastructure spending does not inadvertently create new vulnerabilities.

Nepal should also expand multi-hazard early warning systems nationwide, with particular attention to remote and high-risk communities. Investments in weather monitoring, forecasting, communication networks and community preparedness should be accompanied by clear evacuation protocols and regular drills so that warnings lead to timely action.

Greater financing for local adaptation is equally important. Municipalities and provincial authorities need predictable resources and technical support to implement locally identified adaptation priorities. A dedicated mountain resilience and glacial-risk management fund could further strengthen Nepal's capacity to address risks associated with glacial lakes, mountain ecosystems and climate-induced hazards.

At the same time, ecosystem-based adaptation should be integrated into land-use planning. Protecting forests, wetlands, watersheds and other natural systems can complement engineered infrastructure and reduce exposure to floods, erosion and landslides. Such measures should be incorporated into development decisions rather than treated as separate environmental initiatives.

Social protection must also form part of Nepal's adaptation strategy. Climate shocks disproportionately affect households with limited assets and income security. Strengthening social protection systems and ensuring that support can be scaled up rapidly after disasters would help vulnerable households recover without falling deeper into poverty.

Finally, Nepal should strengthen climate-data sharing and regional cooperation. Better access to reliable climate and hazard data can improve risk assessment, early warning and infrastructure planning. Cooperation with neighbouring countries is particularly important for managing risks that cross national borders, including river floods and glacial hazards.

The GGA is still evolving, but Nepal does not need to wait for every global mechanism to be finalised. The country can use the framework to accelerate investments and reforms that are already essential to its development. For Nepal, the question is no longer whether adaptation is necessary, but how quickly it can be turned into practical resilience.

description: Early warning system Nepal's top priority: PM Shah  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
An early warning system for disasters will be implemented as a "top priority" in Nepal, said Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Saturday (September 19, 2026).

Why WFP has called Nepal flood relief one of its toughest missions | Explained

The Bhotekoshi flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, killing over 1,400 people and leaving over 6,000 missing as of Friday (September 18, 2026).

Experts believe many lives would have been saved if they had proper warning.

Speaking at a Constitution Day programme at Tundikel Open Ground on Saturday (September 19, 2026), PM Shah said, "Special emphasis will be laid on risk reduction, preparedness, and response. The disaster early warning system will be implemented as a top priority." PM Shah also expressed gratitude to all friendly nations, the international community and organisations, private sector, civil servants and the people of the country who assisted in disaster management, noting that the "loss and damage caused by the Bhotekoshi flood were unimaginable and irreparable for us”.

Nepal flash flood death toll surges to 1,410; over 6,100 still missing

Speaking about the country's economy, the Prime Minister said that the government would work to promote innovation and entrepreneurship and the creation of a knowledge-based economy by integrating artificial intelligence, digital technology and cyber security.

Citing the Digital Governance Action Plan, Mr. Shah said that the good governance demanded by the youth would also be ensured through technology. Stating that good governance, development, prosperity and social justice are the aspirations of citizens, he said, "The government's each step is, and will remain, directed towards realising these very aspirations."

Nepal flood reconstruction bill to be $4.78 bn: foreign ministry

The Prime Minister said that competitive multi-party democracy, human rights and the rule of law are the foundations of national life. "This Constitution has made one promise before the Nepali citizen that is building an equitable society based on unity amidst diversity, an end to all forms of discrimination, on development, prosperity and social justice," he said.

"The federal government is committed to achieving the shared goal of national development based on cooperation, coexistence, and coordination among the federal, provincial, and local levels," Mr. Shah said.

Eleven years ago, on Ashwin 3, 2072 (Bikram Sambat calendar), Nepal promulgated its new Constitution, which typically corresponds to mid-September on the Gregorian calendar.

title: Langtang Flood Update: 1,453 Dead, 6,664 Missing - Explorersweb »
description: Langtang Flood Update: 1,453 Dead, 6,664 Missing  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
The flood and debris flow that started on Langtang Lirung on August 26, then struck the Kyirong Valley, has killed at least 1,453 people in Nepal and Tibet. Another 6,664 remain missing.

Nepal accounts for most of the dead and missing: 1,410 killed and 6,145 unaccounted for. In Tibet’s Kyirong County, officials have reported 43 dead and 519 missing.

Hundreds of the missing on both sides of the border are foreigners, including pilgrims going to Mount Kailash, traders, hydroelectric workers, trekkers, and travelers using one of the busiest land crossings between China and Nepal.

How it fell

Rock and ice broke away from the north flank of 7,227m Langtang Lirung, triggering a massive debris flow down the Lhende Khola River toward the border.

The landslide began around 5,200m and fell more than 2,200 vertical meters. Moving swiftly, it traveled 20 to 22km in just seven minutes. The impact completely destroyed the buildings along the Tibet–Nepal border, the road to Gyirong Port, and the Rasuwagadhi crossing.

The collapse was initially reported as a small earthquake but was later classified as a landslide that triggered a magnitude 5.2 seismic shock wave. Downstream, the resulting flood filled hydroelectric tunnels with mud, wrecked bridges, and flattened villages along the river. While the debris bypassed the main Langtang trekking valley, it tore through the trench between Kyirong and Rasuwa before surging down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli Rivers.

Glacier collapse on the North Face of Langtang. Photo: Google Earth via Nepalitimes.com

The destruction was immediate and concentrated within the narrow valley floor.

The figures are still changing. Officials say the missing-person lists may include unidentified bodies and people already found. Identification has been slow. Some bodies were carried 240km downriver into India.

title: Nepali MMA star Yuki Angdembe beats China’s Buhuogubu in JCK-123 - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepali MMA star Yuki Angdembe beats China’s Buhuogubu in JCK-123  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s Yuki “The Gurkha” Angdembe defeated China’s Buhuogubu “The Yi Eagle” by unanimous decision at Jue Cheng King (JCK) Fight Night-123 in Luliang, China, on Saturday.

Angdembe and Buhuogubu started the three-round fight, each of five minutes, with kicks and punches. It was not until the last minute of the first round that Angdembe used his strength: grappling.

And Angdembe continued with his wrestling moves at the start of the second round, keeping Buhuogubu on the ground, aiming to finish the fight either with a knockout or a submission.

However, Buhuogubu seemed prepared for Angdembe’s tactics. Despite Angdembe landing some good punches, Buhuogubu still found ways to stay in the fight.

When the third and final round commenced, Angdembe and Buhuogubu started with a hug, with both fighters showing respect to each other.

The third round again saw the duo struggling against each other on the ground, but with Angdembe having the upper hand. Angdembe had his Soma Fight Club colleague Zack “Bahadur” Bennett in his corner, continuously motivating him.

By the end of the fight, Angdembe’s victory was a foregone conclusion. It was announced that the three judges had each scored 27-30 in favour of Angdembe.

Angdembe celebrated the win draped in a Nepali flag and wearing a rudraksha mala alongside Bennett, who was wearing a waistcoat made of Nepali dhaka fabric.

title: Fees keep Nepal-Israel farm, care worker deals on hold - The Kathmandu Post
description: Fees keep Nepal-Israel farm, care worker deals on hold  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
A dispute over recruitment and service fees has stalled two proposed agreements to send Nepali workers to Israel’s agricultural and home-based care sectors, despite demand for labour in both areas.

Under draft protocols sent to Nepal, agricultural workers would have to pay an Israeli agency 3,825 shekels, including VAT, or about Rs193,000. Workers going into home-based caregiving would pay 6,443 shekels, or about Rs325,000, also including VAT.

Nepal has objected to the fees because they do not fit its policy of government-led recruitment designed to minimise costs for migrant workers. Israel, however, says private agencies are legally authorised to charge foreign workers for services related to their placement and management.

Under the proposed arrangements, Nepali workers would be selected and sent to Israel through government mechanisms. Once there, Israeli manpower agencies would take responsibility for assigning them to farms or households and managing their employment.

Workers would also have to cover other costs, including air tickets, medical examinations, English-language tests, visas, labour-related fees and insurance.

For agricultural workers, the draft protocol requires the 3,825-shekel fee to be deposited into the agency’s bank account within one working day of arrival in Israel. The agency would then issue an official receipt.

For home-based caregivers, the proposed 6,443-shekel fee would be paid in three instalments. Workers would pay 3,943 shekels, including VAT, within three days of arrival, followed by 1,250 shekels at the end of their 26th month and another 1,250 shekels at the end of their 38th month.

Israel says the fees cover management, welfare and administrative services. Its Population and Immigration Authority has long involved authorised private agencies in registering foreign workers and managing their employment with employers in the agricultural and home-care sectors.

“Whether workers have to pay a service fee is linked to policy. We are discussing this condition with Israel,” a Labour Ministry official told the Post. “We are saying that agricultural and home-based care workers should be recruited under the same institutional model currently used for caregivers.”

Israel sent the two draft protocols to Nepal about a year ago. The dispute has delayed their finalisation.

Israeli Ambassador to Nepal Shmulik Arie Bass has said Nepal’s hesitation is costing Nepali workers employment opportunities. Speaking to journalists during a recent visit to Pokhara, Bass said Nepal was reluctant to sign a protocol under which workers could earn about $130,000 over 63 months, or roughly Rs20 million.

“The service fee is not paid to human traffickers or brokers. It is paid to companies designated by the Israeli government through tenders for services including health insurance, so there should be no doubt about it,” Bass said.

He also said Israeli law, enacted by parliament in 2001, requires the fee to be paid electronically within three days of a worker’s arrival.

Nepal already has a separate protocol under which caregivers are sent to institutions providing long-term care to elderly and disabled people in Israel. That arrangement is different from home-based caregiving.

On July 16, 1,115 Nepalis were selected through a lottery to work under the institutional care programme. Seventy-five percent of those selected were men and 25 percent women. The Department of Foreign Employment is sending them in groups.

Applications have also been invited for another 1,464 positions under the programme, with the deadline set for October 12.

Bass said the number of Nepali workers entering Israel through the institutional care programme remains limited, while demand for workers in agriculture and home-based care is much higher.

Israel has authorised up to 70,000 work permits for foreign agricultural workers. Israeli officials said about 49,000 foreign workers were employed in agriculture at the beginning of 2026.

Thailand, Sri Lanka and Malawi are among the main sources of agricultural workers, while Israel has also reached agreements with Cambodia and Ecuador. In 2025, Israel agreed with Thailand to bring in 13,000 agricultural workers.

title: Nepal seeks climate funds as scientists link floods to global warming - The Climate Watch
description: Nepal seeks climate funds as scientists link floods to global warming  The Climate Watch
publisher.title: The Climate Watch
full_article:
Nepal is seeking loss-and-damage funding after a climate-linked Himalayan disaster, highlighting the widening gap between vulnerable countries’ needs and available international finance.

Nepal is seeking international funding to help recover from a devastating disaster in the Himalayan Rasuwa district, arguing that climate change helped create the conditions for the collapse and that the country should not bear the cost alone.

A two-square-kilometre mass of glacier ice and rock collapsed from Langtang Lirung mountain in the days, weeks, months and years before a debris flow swept into the valley, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving another 5,000 missing.

An international team of researchers that rapidly assessed the disaster for World Weather Attribution, an initiative examining the role of climate change in specific extreme weather events, concluded that global warming had helped condition the slope for failure.

For Nepal and other small nations, such attribution studies provide important evidence in efforts to secure funding to cope with the effects of a warming planet.

Nepal’s ministries of finance and environment sent a joint letter on August 31 to the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established in 2022 to support victims of the climate crisis.

The government estimates that recovery from the Rasuwa disaster will cost $4.8 billion, equivalent to more than 11 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product. It is seeking $20 million, the maximum amount countries can request from the fund, for immediate recovery and preparations for future disasters.

Nepal presented the request as an issue of climate justice rather than aid. Its foreign minister said the country had paid “the ultimate price for a global crisis [it] did not create.”

The attribution study found that atmospheric warming of 2 degrees Celsius, well above the global average, had thawed permafrost holding cracked rock walls together, while glacier ice had thinned and retreated. Rain was also falling at elevations where it had previously fallen only as snow.

Rainwater and meltwater then lubricated fractures deep within the rock, further destabilising the slope.

In order to rebuild what was destroyed by floods, Nepal estimates they will need $4.8 billion. Country officials are requesting $20 million from the U.N.’s Loss and Damage fund. Photo: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP, Getty Images

“We conclude this was a geologically vulnerable slope,” said Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands and a coauthor of the study, during a press conference. “But it was destabilized further by glacier retreat and permafrost thaw, and with excessive meltwater and exceptional warmth in the final period before the failure.”

The warming was driven by human-generated greenhouse gas emissions. The Rasuwa disaster is “yet another warning sign,” the report said, that climate change is transforming high mountain environments and creating conditions for cascading hazards.

Andrew Pershing, a climate scientist not involved in the study and chief program officer at Climate Central, which also conducts attribution research, compared climate change’s influence on the Rasuwa disaster with increasingly frequent and severe wildfires in the American West.

In both cases, “climate is this preconditioner that’s putting weight on the scale towards the event,” he said. “It’s making these places much more unstable and risky to be around.”

The researchers said Nepal’s flood warning system was unable to match the speed and volume of the debris flow that surged down the valley.

“Events of this magnitude ultimately exceed the limits of adaptation,” they wrote, arguing that international “recovery and reconstruction support in impacted communities has now become an unavoidable part of climate response.”

Nepal produces less than 0.1 percent of annual global greenhouse gas emissions but is experiencing the effects of climate-warming gases firsthand, said Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Center for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University’s Institute of Engineering in Nepal.

Because Nepal has contributed so little to the emissions that helped create the conditions for the disaster, its leaders do not believe the country should be solely responsible for paying for the recovery.

Scientists in Nepal have long known that the country is vulnerable to rising temperatures. Nepal regularly experiences glacial-lake outburst floods, which have also been scientifically attributed to climate change.

“We have all the evidence,” Adhikari said. “So, of course we need compensation, we need funds to combat climate change in the name of mitigation or adaptation,” he said.

Recovery efforts will include rebuilding infrastructure such as roads and hydropower plants, as well as relocating and rebuilding communities.

Nepal also wants to establish new monitoring systems capable of identifying and tracking unstable rock slopes and glaciers and providing timely warnings to downstream communities, in an effort to prevent a disaster of the same scale from happening again.

Since 2022, wealthy nations have pledged $822 million to the UN’s loss and damage fund. But 119 countries have since requested assistance totalling $2.8 billion.

Early proposals for what eventually became the fund were framed as a form of global insurance, under which countries would contribute according to their emissions. Fierce debate followed, however, and major high-emitting countries in the European Union and the United States rejected liability for damage caused by their greenhouse gas emissions in other countries.

The current voluntary fund, explicitly based on international cooperation, emerged from that compromise.

But the arrangement has left governments and communities that contributed little to climate change struggling to meet the costs of its impacts. The UN fund remains far short of what Nepal needs.

As communities affected by climate change seek compensation, courts in the United States and Europe have seen a rise in climate litigation in recent years.

Attribution science, including the recently published World Weather Attribution report, is increasingly being used to connect emissions from specific polluters with particular harms.

In 2023, Multnomah County in Oregon sued more than a dozen oil companies over their role in the deadly 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, which climate attribution research had found was “virtually impossible” without climate change.

Worldwide, 3,600 such cases have been filed in 62 jurisdictions and 28 international courts. No plaintiff has yet won a liability case.

Scientists have nevertheless become better and faster at determining whether and how climate change contributed to individual disasters. Climate models can now establish definitively that a particular heatwave would not have occurred without human-caused warming and can then trace contributions to that warming to specific polluters.

But attribution science is more difficult outside Europe and North America, where long-term datasets are generally more robust. The challenge is particularly acute for complex events involving cascading hazards, such as the Rasuwa disaster.

“Cause and effect can get very murky in these events,” Pershing said.

Pre-existing weaknesses in the bedrock, climate-related factors and potentially the lingering effects of the nearby 2015 Gorkha earthquake all contributed to the collapse.

Scientists lack subsurface temperature measurements, data on water pressure within fractures and other key information needed to quantify precisely how much climate change contributed. Doing so would be “almost impossible,” Immerzeel said.

Scientists nevertheless say the disaster in Nepal shows strong signs of a rapidly warming planet and points to a growing risk of more sudden and devastating events in mountainous regions.

“The climate is changing in the Himalayas, and it’s not only the fate of the Nepali Himalayan people. There are more than two billion people living downstream, all these places are in increasing vulnerability as these events are increasing,” Adhikari said.

“We are in existential threat due to climate change. We need to save our civilization in high-mountain Asia.”

title: Letter to the editor: The warning from Nepal is loud enough to reach Utah - Deseret News
description: Letter to the editor: The warning from Nepal is loud enough to reach Utah  Deseret News
publisher.title: Deseret News
full_article:
Recent climate news has been bleak, from destruction in Nepal to warnings that the world is likely to exceed the 1.5 degrees warming target.

Small variations in degrees sound abstract, but they translate into more deadly heat, severe storms, flooding and threats to food supplies and ecosystems. Fatalism, however, is a mistake. Every fraction of a degree — and every ton of heat-trapping pollution we prevent — matters.

Here in Utah, climate change looks different, but the physics is the same. The Deseret News has reported our warmest winter on record and record-low snowpack .

Fortunately, solutions are growing here, too. Utah has abundant solar and geothermal resources, and nearly 49,000 clean-energy jobs. Solar recently generated more Utah electricity than any other source . Expanding clean energy can create jobs, strengthen our grid, attract rural investment and clean our air.

1 Comment

Climate change is not ideological. Heat-trapping gases warm the atmosphere regardless of politics. Ask Utah’s federal legislators who to enact practical, bipartisan climate solutions that reduce polluting emissions while strengthening our economy and energy security.

The warning from Nepal is loud enough to reach Utah — if we choose to hear it.

Karen Jackson,

Salt Lake City, Utah
